What is something that you think makes someone interesting?
Personally, I find that anyone with a vast knowledge of a seemingly meaningless topic is interesting. That's their thing.

I like people who are passionate about a science and know how to explain some of it to others 'like they're five". It means that they've probably put a lot of thought into it and love to see others become fascinated by it, too, even if those others aren't as passionate about it as they are. They're able to make something that might look too complex and daunting into something interesting, and it's a great way to get more people into science.
I believe it was Einstein that said something along the lines of "If you can't explain a complex topic simply, you do not truly understand it.".

I think being well traveled and well read make people interesting. Although I understand that due to financial constraints many people cannot necessarily travel often or widely, but a library card is free and books are widely available for free on the internet, so there is no reason everyone should not be, at least to some degree or on a particular subject, well read.

Someone who has demonstrated that they are they're own person, that they're authentic. What I mean by that is that they are free of gimmicks that a lot of people use as crutches to form a mask or a fake identity. Someone who is not afraid to go against the grain, but not just because they think it's edgy or hip.
I think this is definitely something I can agree with. I've never been able to quite word it so well though.
I find people who own knives and have an exacting knowledge of the preparation of human meat interesting. For real, though, I did have this one friend...
I really like people with a sharp wit who can take shit and give it back just as good. I tend to playfully tease my friends, and I've found these are the type of people I build the best rapport with.

Someone that can talk about art. I love a good in depth conversation about art. I feel that the skill easily transfers to a lot of important areas in life. The ability to relate to others, to form their own ideas, to understand the context of an idea, to be able to simply appreciate a variety of beautiful things. An interesting person will be able to appreciate the girth of artistic expressions. Art is not just paintings in Le Louvre or Mozart's music, but they are essential pieces of significance. House music is art and I want to know what you think of it in full artistic context.
People who aren't right in the head. Yeah, sure, they aren't trustworthy and whatnot, but they aren't bland.

I've been playing vidya a long fucking time, and have a couple experiences that have stayed with me my entire life.

Metroid

This was one of the defining moments of my life as a gamer. It was Christmas Eve, 1986 I believe, the year that Nintendo was the big thing and you could buy the big box set with the gun and the little robot. My second cousin (in his 20s) got that box for Christmas and my father and I went to his place (just across the street from where our family Christmas Eve party was happening, to check it out. I was 5 or 6.

Metroid was the game my cousin was showing off. I'd played Atari and Colecovision games before and thought I knew about games, but it blew my mind when he RAN TO THE LEFT to get the morphball. Waaaaaat? I was impressed by this deviation from what I considered the norm but what got me, and permanently affected me, was what happened next.

I noticed there was no score.

"Where is the score?" I asked my cousin.

"There is no score," he replied. "You just have to get to the end."

And that was it, that was all it took to shatter my preconceptions of videogames, for my small child's brain to make the leap from 'videogames are games' to 'videogames are ADVENTURES.' It was such a paradigm shift for me that it literally changed my life and I will never forget it, it was a perfect moment for a gamer to have.

Ultima Underworld: The Stygian Abyss

I could go on forever about this game but let's just say it established expectations for the genre of firsperson-RPGs that has never since been exceeded. Even the best dungeon crawlers and FPRPGs fall short of the highwater mark UU set way back in 1994. A spiritual successor by some of the original devs is currently in development and I have high hopes for it indeed.

Fallout 1

I played Fallout 1 when it was still new, bought the weird oblong box with the flip-up cover and everything (on sale for like 10 bucks a couple months after release). I'd read it was the RPG of the year but the beginning of the game (stabbing rats for 15 minutes) was underwhelming and I gave up. I tried it again a couple days later, committed to winning, and I got into the game proper, which was, well, you probably know, amazing.

The lasting impression was two fold: first, Fallout was the first (and is still one of the only) games where your intelligence score effects conversation options, which meant traditional min-maxing was pointless. Second, I beat the game but totally bypassed the final boss, because my character was a thief and snuck into the basement of the last area, armed a nuclear bomb, and escaped. I didn't even KNOW there was a final boss until a friend asked me about it weeks later. I've never played a game since that let me do that.

Halflife

I played Halflife before it released; the 'OEM' version was included with certain videocards allowing you to play right up to, I believe, the Surface Tension chapter. My friend had acquired it and, well, it was college so we did a bunch of acid and proceeded to check the game out. We could tell from the training that the game was awesome but what happened next is what I will never forget.

We started up the game proper and were on the monorail. I sat back, lit a cigarette, and we watched as the monorail did its thing. Maybe a minute into the sequence I went to flick my cigarette, accidentally hit the mouse and... HOLY SHIT THE SCREEN MOVED.

And we realized, we were ON the fucking monorail. We could walk around, look around, focus on whatever. It can not be overstated how amazing this was to us at the time, not because of the drugs (though they helped) but because this was the first time anything like this ever happened in a game. The entire introductory sequence with Freeman going to work... it was amazing, there was nothing like it, and it changed my expectations of videogames forever.

Homeworld

The first game that made me cry. The ending was just so beautiful.

I could go on and on and on, I have been affected by so many games, but this is long enough I think, ha.

My first huge battle in Planetside 2's beta. My friend got me a code that day, and was showing me around Indar as TR. Out of nowhere, all the command chat was spamming for everyone to pull back to the main base, spawn some armor, and get ready to roll. Never before, and never again did I see hundreds of ground vehicles gathered up for a single push. When the signal was given, we rolled out, a convoy hundreds strong and trailing along like a bunch of ants.

We pushed up through a canyon, which then opened out like a funnel. The instant we exited the funnel, NC greeted us with their own army of air vehicles. The ensuing battle was pure chaos. Sunderers were veering to the side of the road, letting the gunners have a good shot at the aircraft. Some tanks and ATVs kept pushing forward, despite the kill box those fighters had set up. In the end, our push was a complete failure. But that moment solidified my love of Planetside 2's large scale combat.

Since the beta, Planetside 2's battles turned from exciting open field conflicts to CQB meat grinders. I hop on every now and then, hoping the combat's changed. It's getting better, but still hasn't hit that magical point again.
